summary.alternatives_overview.extracted_value: The environmental impact statement analyzed six alternatives: (1) no action (keep the existing formula); (2) eliminate the population-mileage formula and define each city case-by-case; (3) an even more expansive formula (Arthur D. Little proposed 5 to 30 miles by city size); (4) a 'ring approach' measuring the radius from the city center instead of the current 'contour approach' measuring from corporate limits; (5) a formula 50 percent larger for cities with physical barriers like oceans, mountains, or deserts; and (6) using Census Bureau Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas (SMSAs — county-based groupings requiring a central city of at least 50,000). The Commission rejected SMSAs as too broad because they include entire counties regardless of population density, rejected center-point measurement because most cities lack a commonly accepted center, rejected case-by-case adjudication as too slow, and rejected a physical-limitations correction as not administratively feasible. Commenters also proposed treating pairs like San Francisco/Oakland as 'twin cities' with combined populations and exempting specialized carriers (bulk tank trucks, household goods movers, initial-movement auto transporters) — the Commission adopted twin-city treatment for twelve pairs but rejected the specialty-carrier carve-outs as contrary to uniform regulation.

summary.environmental_impact.extracted_value: The Commission prepared a draft environmental impact statement under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and a final statement in Appendix C, and concluded that zone expansion will not harm the environment. The main projected benefit is a reduction in 'interlining' (where a long-haul carrier hands off freight to a local carrier at a terminal), which the Commission expects to cut truck mileage, fuel use, and emissions of the four main motor-vehicle pollutants — carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, photochemical oxidants, and hydrocarbons — consistent with the Clean Air Act of 1970. The main adverse effect analyzed is that a larger exempt market may draw more local unregulated carriers, producing empty mileage, lower load factors, more fuel use, and more urban traffic congestion until competition stabilizes. Commenters warned that industrial development in the ring between the old and new Minneapolis-St. Paul boundaries could damage water bodies, groundwater recharge areas, wetlands, agricultural lands, and habitat for rare species; the Commission responded that there is not enough evidence linking zone expansion to sprawl and that such development is properly controlled by local land-use rules and existing state and federal wetlands regulations. Safety concerns about hazardous liquids and dry bulk commodities moving in unregulated urban operations were referred to the Federal Highway Administration.
summary.environmental_impact.evidence_quote: Industrial development in the ring between boundaries of the present Commercial Zone of Minneapolis-St. Paul and the proposed 15 mile zone would have extremely serious adverse environmental consequences in such areas as water bodies and water courses, ground water recharge areas, wet lands, soils, agricultural lands, and unique or endangered plants and animals.

summary.overview.extracted_value: The Interstate Commerce Commission is issuing a final rule that enlarges the 'commercial zones' and 'terminal areas' around U.S. cities — the geographic rings within which trucking companies and freight forwarders can pick up and deliver freight without needing full federal operating authority. The rule replaces a 1940s-era 2-to-5-mile formula with a graduated population-mileage formula that reaches 20 miles for cities of 1 million or more, with custom zones for places like New York, Los Angeles, and St. Louis and combined zones for 'twin cities' such as Minneapolis-St. Paul. Alternatives considered and rejected include keeping the old formula, defining each city's zone case-by-case, using Census Bureau Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas (county-based groupings the Commission found too broad), and measuring the radius from a city's center rather than its corporate limits. The Commission prepared a draft and final environmental impact statement under the National Environmental Policy Act and concluded that zone expansion will not harm the environment, though commenters warned of more trucks on urban roads and possible sprawl into wetlands and farmland in rings like the one between the old and new Minneapolis-St. Paul boundaries. Public response split sharply: shippers, port authorities, chambers of commerce, and freight forwarders overwhelmingly supported expansion, while small short-haul carriers, specialized carriers, and 143 of 144 individual commenters opposed it, and two commissioners dissented, calling the result 'tantamount to a deregulatory effort.'

summary.project_description.extracted_value: The Interstate Commerce Commission is finalizing a rule (Ex Parte No. MC-37 (Sub-No. 26), amending 49 CFR Parts 1041, 1048, and 1049) that enlarges the 'commercial zones' and 'terminal areas' around U.S. cities — the geographic rings within which motor carriers and freight forwarders can pick up and deliver freight under a partial exemption from federal economic regulation in sections 203(b)(8) and 202(c) of the Interstate Commerce Act. The rule replaces the mid-1940s population-mileage formula with a larger graduated formula: for example, cities under 2,500 people get a 3-mile radius from city limits, cities of 100,000–199,999 get 8 miles, and cities of 1 million or more get 20 miles. Special custom-drawn boundaries apply to New York, Los Angeles (which abolishes the separate Harbor zone), St. Louis, Washington D.C., Pittsburgh, and twelve 'twin city' pairs (such as Minneapolis-St. Paul and Kansas City, Mo.-Kansas City, Kans.) that are treated as a single municipality. The rules take effect 90 days after Federal Register publication.
summary.project_description.evidence_quote: the rules adopted herein shall become effective 90 days from the date of publication of the attached notice in the Federal Register
summary.project_description.note: Key claims verified: Ex Parte No. MC-37 (Sub-No. 26) amending 49 CFR Parts 1041, 1048, 1049 (page 200); population-mileage formula figures (pages 5, 203, 214); sections 203(b)(8) and 202(c) exemption framing (pages 6, 53, 117); Los Angeles Harbor zone abolished (page 106); twin cities list including Minneapolis-St. Paul and Kansas City pairs (pages 118, 211-212); 90-day effective date (page 132).

summary.public_response.extracted_value: Response split sharply by group. Of 121 shipper and local commenters, 120 favored expansion; all three state agencies supported it; but 143 of 144 individual commenters (mostly employees of regulated motor carriers) opposed it. Motor carriers divided along size lines — long-haul and irregular-route carriers generally supported expansion, while small short-haul carriers argued it amounted to deregulation, would divert their traffic to new unregulated entrants, and constituted an unconstitutional Fifth Amendment 'taking' of the value of their operating certificates. The Freight Forwarders Institute, the U.S. Department of Transportation, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, the Pennjerdel Corporation, and the chambers of commerce of Dallas, Houston, and Pittsburgh supported expansion; the Environmental Protection Agency did not object but asked for more air quality detail, and the Department of the Interior offered no comments. Several carriers demanded formal oral hearings and cross-examination and objected to Federal Register notice; the Commission rejected these procedural demands, holding that neither the Administrative Procedure Act nor the Constitution requires an oral hearing in a rulemaking on legislative facts. Commissioner Brown dissented, and Commissioner Hardin (joined by Chairman Stafford and Commissioner Murphy) dissented that the record did not justify the new formula, calling the result 'tantamount to a deregulatory effort.'
